answer:
**Assumptions and cost**

- **Shokri et al. (shadow models).** The adversary trains shadow models on data from a similar distribution. Because the adversary knows which points each shadow model trained on, it can label confidence vectors as member or non-member and train a classifier on them (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [7]). A later summary states two assumptions: shadow models share the target's structure, and their training data share its distribution (Rezaei and Liu 2020 [6]). Salem et al. report experimentally that one shadow model and one attack model give performance very similar to 10 shadow models and 100 attack models. They also report that the attack works with different architectures and with data from other distributions, and even without any shadow model, using a threshold on the maximum posterior or entropy (Salem et al. 2018 [1]; Rezaei and Liu 2020 [6]).
- **Yeom et al. (loss threshold).** The attacker makes one query to the model and needs to know only the average training loss. Shokri's attack, by contrast, needs considerable computation and knowledge of the training algorithm (Yeom et al. 2017 [23]). Yeom's attack thresholds the loss or the confidence in the correct class (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [14]; Jayaraman and Evans 2022 [24]). A related label-only baseline predicts "member" when the model classifies the point correctly. Its accuracy is 1/2 + (acc_train − acc_test)/2, so it directly reflects the train–test gap (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [7]).

**Strength: average-case results**

- Yeom et al. report experimentally that, when the size parameter matches Shokri's, their attack has the same recall and only slightly lower precision (Yeom et al. 2017 [23]).
- Jayaraman et al. report that Shokri's original fixed threshold of 0.5 gives about 50% membership advantage but a PPV of about 67% on Purchase-100X. With their threshold-selection procedure, Shokri's PPV exceeds 73%, comparable to Yeom's (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [5]).
- Which attack wins depends on the dataset. Shokri achieves higher PPV on Texas-100 and RCV1X, while Yeom is better on CIFAR-100 (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [5]).

**Strength: low false-positive rates**

- Carlini et al. argue that balanced accuracy is an inadequate metric. Their LOSS attack on a CIFAR-10 model has 60% balanced accuracy. Yet on the 1% of samples with the lowest loss, it is correct only 48% of the time. It is therefore a strong non-membership inference attack but practically useless for confidently inferring membership (Carlini et al. 2021 [25]).
- Their LOSS baseline reaches 0.0% TPR at 0.1% FPR. Global-threshold attacks do not succeed at low FPR when identifying members (Carlini et al. 2021 [11][26]).
- Calibrating per example, which needs shadow models, raises TPR at 0.1% FPR substantially. Their full online attack reaches 8.4% (Carlini et al. 2021 [11]). Carlini et al. also note that this improvement is not captured by balanced accuracy or AUC (Carlini et al. 2021 [17]).
- Rezaei and Liu report that confidence-based attacks, including shadow-model ones, often suffer from high false-alarm rates (FAR) even on strongly overfitted models (Rezaei and Liu 2020 [28]).

- **Shokri et al. (shadow models).**

  - Two assumptions are usually named. The shadow models share the target's structure, and their training data comes from the same distribution as the target's (Rezaei and Liu 2020 [2]; Salem et al. 2018 [7]).
  - In Jayaraman et al.'s and Jayaraman and Evans's reimplementations, the attack uses five shadow models with the target's architecture and a two-hidden-layer (64-unit) inference model (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [3]; Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [8]).
- **Yeom et al. (loss threshold).**
  - The attacker makes one query and needs to know only the average training loss. No attack model is trained, and no knowledge of the training algorithm is required (Yeom et al. 2017 [5]).
  - A record is called a member if its loss is below the expected training loss (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [8]).
  - A label-only version, the "gap attack", predicts membership when the model classifies the point correctly. Its accuracy is 1/2 + (acc_train − acc_test)/2, so it reflects the train–test gap (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [6]).
- **Relaxations of Shokri.** Salem et al. report experimentally that one shadow model suffices, and that shadow data from a different distribution still works (Salem et al. 2018 [1]; Rezaei and Liu 2020 [2]). They also report that a simple threshold on the maximum posterior or its entropy needs no shadow model (Salem et al. 2018 [1]; Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [6]). This moves the Shokri family toward Yeom-style threshold attacks.

**Strength (empirical findings)**

- Yeom et al. report that with the same size parameter as Shokri et al., their attack has the same recall and only slightly lower precision, at far lower computational cost (Yeom et al. 2017 [5]).
- Jayaraman et al. find that results depend on the dataset. Shokri achieves higher PPV than Yeom on Texas-100 and RCV1X, while Yeom is better on CIFAR-100 (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [3]).
- Shokri's default 0.5 threshold gives close to 50% membership advantage but a PPV of about 67% on Purchase-100X. Choosing the threshold to maximize PPV raises it above 73%, comparable to Yeom (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [3]).

**Shadow-model attack (Shokri et al.)**
- The attacker trains shadow models to mimic the target's behavior. Their outputs on known members and non-members form a labeled dataset for the attack models, one per class (Salem et al. 2018 [1]; Song and Mittal 2020 [7]).
- Two main assumptions are that the shadow models share the target's structure and that their training data comes from the same distribution as the target's (Salem et al. 2018 [1]; Rezaei and Liu 2020 [4]).
- The attacker queries the target as a black box and uses the confidence scores (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [6]).
- It relies on the target's confidence being higher on training instances, which is typically a consequence of a generalization gap (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [6]).
- Salem et al. report experimentally that these requirements can be relaxed. One shadow model suffices, and the architecture and data distribution need not match (Salem et al. 2018 [1][2]; Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [6]). A simple threshold on max confidence needs no shadow model at all (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [8]).

**Loss-threshold attack (Yeom et al.)**
- The attacker needs access to the target model and its average training loss (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [6][25]).
- It classifies a record as a member if its loss is below that average (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [6][25]).
- Yeom et al. contrast this with Shokri's attack. Theirs needs one query and no shadow-model training, whereas Shokri's requires considerable computation and knowledge of the training algorithm (Yeom et al. 2017 [24]).

- Yeom et al. analyze advantage as a function of overfitting. This shows that generalization behavior is a strong predictor of vulnerability (Yeom et al. 2017 [15]).

## Strength

- **Early comparison:** Yeom et al. report experimentally that, at the same size parameter, their attacker has the same recall and slightly lower precision than Shokri's (Yeom et al. 2017 [24]).
- **PPV comparison:** Jayaraman et al. tuned the decision thresholds of both attacks.

  - Shokri has a higher PPV than Yeom on Texas-100 and RCV1X, while Yeom outperforms Shokri on CIFAR-100 (Jayaraman et al. 2020 [12]).

question: How do shadow-model attacks (Shokri et al.) differ from loss-threshold attacks (Yeom et al.) in assumptions and strength?
answer:
## Assumptions

**Shokri et al. (shadow models)**
- The attacker has black-box access. It queries the target and gets a probability vector, which is passed with the true label to an attack model that outputs in/out (Shokri et al. 2016 [1]).
- It trains shadow models on the same ML platform, with training data of the same format as the target's but disjoint from it (Shokri et al. 2016 [1]).
- It trains a binary attack classifier, one per output class, on the shadow models' outputs, labelled in/out (Shokri et al. 2016 [4][5]).
- In Yeom et al.'s summary, this needs the ability to train shadow models, i.e. knowledge of the input distribution and model type, and the attack "must train hundreds of shadow models" (Yeom et al. 2017 [9]).
- Shokri et al. report experimentally that the attack tolerates noisy shadow data. It can also work with synthetic shadow data, with precision 0.935 on real, 0.795 on marginal-based synthetic and 0.895 on model-based synthetic data (purchase dataset, Google-trained model) (Shokri et al. 2016 [22]).

**Yeom et al. (loss/threshold adversaries)**
- Yeom et al. say their attacker makes one query to the model and needs only the average training loss L_S (Yeom et al. 2017 [23][9]).
- The bounded-loss adversary assumes only that the loss is bounded by a constant B (Yeom et al. 2017 [11]). The Gaussian-error adversary assumes knowledge of the error distributions, for example σ_S and σ_D (Yeom et al. 2017 [10]).
- Formal result: the bounded-loss adversary's membership advantage is R_gen(A)/B. In classification with 0-1 loss and B = 1, the advantage equals the generalization error (Yeom et al. 2017 [10]).

## Strength

- **Yeom et al.'s own comparison (empirical):** recall is 0.99 for both. Their attack has slightly lower precision, but needs far fewer resources and less background knowledge (Yeom et al. 2017 [9][23]). The table lists precision 0.505/0.694/0.874 for Yeom et al. against 0.517/0.72–0.74/0.99 for Shokri et al. on MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 (Yeom et al. 2017 [9]).
- **Low-FPR evaluation (Carlini et al.):** they argue attacks should be judged by TPR at low FPR (e.g. ≤0.1%) and find that most prior attacks perform poorly under that metric (Carlini et al. 2021 [14]). They report that the shadow-model attack is much more expensive than the LOSS attack but does not perform significantly better at low FPR (Carlini et al. 2021 [15]). Mattern et al. likewise note that the LOSS attack does badly at very low FPR (Mattern et al. 2023 [12]).
- **Theory (Ye et al.):** under certain assumptions and approximations, the likelihood ratio test reduces to comparing the loss with a constant threshold. They stress this is not an optimality guarantee (Ye et al. 2021 [25]). They also note that the shadow-model attack with a label-dependent threshold does not reduce the attacker's uncertainty about the specific target record or model (Ye et al. 2021 [3]).

## Not covered
The sources contain no direct low-FPR comparison of Yeom et al. and Shokri et al. beyond Carlini et al.'s statements about the LOSS attack and the shadow-model attack. The precision/recall table is Yeom et al.'s own comparison. You could use the arXiv search tool to find papers that benchmark the two directly.

question: Do defenses like MemGuard or adversarial regularization actually hold up against adaptive attacks?
answer:
**Short answer:** In these sources, mostly no. Both defenses look strong against the attacks they were originally evaluated on, but follow-up work reports that they weaken substantially against adaptive or different-style attacks. Apart from MemGuard's own paper, the sources do not give numbers for MemGuard under Song and Mittal's adaptive attacks.

**MemGuard**
- Jia et al. report that MemGuard cuts the accuracy of the evaluated attacks to random guessing. For example, on Location this happens at an expected L1 noise of about 0.8 (Jia et al. 2019 [40]). It adds noise to confidence scores without changing the predicted label (Jia et al. 2019 [40]).
- Song and Mittal find that its performance "is greatly degraded with adaptive attacks" and that its original evaluation "lacks a consideration of adaptive adversaries" (Song and Mittal 2020 [34][35]). They recommend that the adversary know the defense and train shadow models that follow it (Song and Mittal 2020 [32]).
- Choquette-Choo et al. report experimentally that MemGuard defends against prior confidence-vector attacks but "offers no protection" against their label-only attacks (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [25]).
  - They attribute MemGuard's earlier success to attacks that were tuned on models without MemGuard and so were not adapted (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [25]).
  - They argue that any defense that only post-processes confidence vectors stays vulnerable to label-only attacks (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [25][9]).
- Li and Zhang's results agree. With MemGuard, the score-based attack AUC drops from 0.8655 to 0.5151 on CIFAR-10 and from 0.755 to 0.513 on Face. The boundary attack stays at 0.8747 and 0.8617, unchanged by MemGuard (Li and Zhang 2020 [7]). They conclude that confidence-score perturbation is infeasible in label-only settings (Li and Zhang 2020 [11]).

**Adversarial regularization**
- Song and Mittal report that it reduces privacy risk only to a limited degree and is no better than early stopping (Song and Mittal 2020 [34][35]).
  - On Purchase100, the Nasr et al. attack gives 51.6% accuracy against the defended model. Their metric-based attacks still reach 55.8–59.5%, and early-stopped models give almost identical numbers (55.9–59.2%) (Song and Mittal 2020 [3]).
  - The defense also costs test accuracy: 80.9% to 76.6% on Purchase100 and 52.3% to 46.4% on Texas100 (Song and Mittal 2020 [3]).
- Choquette-Choo et al. find that label-only attacks significantly outperform the confidence-vector attack against it. Evaluating only against confidence-vector attacks "overestimates the achieved privacy" (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [24]). The defense is not entirely useless, since it limits label-only attacks to within 3 percentage points of the gap attack. When label-only attacks are sufficiently defended, though, its accuracy tradeoff is significantly worse than other defenses (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [24]).
- Nasr et al. themselves report attack accuracy near random guessing against their original attack, for example 51.6% on Purchase100 (Nasr et al. 2018 [21]). That is the non-adaptive baseline that the later papers question.

**Broader context**
- Aerni et al. list weak or non-adaptive attacks as a major pitfall in empirical privacy evaluations (Aerni et al. 2024 [28]). They find that heuristic DP-SGD is the best defense in practice (Aerni et al. 2024 [17]).
- Choquette-Choo et al. report that differential privacy (with transfer learning) gave the strongest defense, though possibly at a cost in test accuracy (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [9]). They also find that DP or strong ℓ2 regularization are the only current defenses that meaningfully reduce leakage (Choquette-Choo et al. 2020 [10]).
- Carlini et al. note that earlier defenses were only shown ineffective on average, not at low FPR. Whether they hold at low FPR is left as an open question (Carlini et al. 2021 [19]).

**Not covered:** the sources have no low-FPR evaluation of MemGuard or adversarial regularization. They also lack Song and Mittal's exact MemGuard numbers under adaptive attack. The arXiv search tool could be used to look for papers on these.

question: Walk through DP-SGD: per-sample clipping, noise addition, and privacy accounting.
answer:
# DP-SGD: clipping, noise, accounting

## 1. The algorithm (one iteration)
1. **Sample a batch.** Each data point is included with probability q = B/N (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Annamalai and Cristofaro 2024 [5]). Abadi et al. (via Ponomareva et al.) describe the batch as sampled with replacement (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]). Nasr et al. describe it as independent per-example inclusion with probability q (Nasr et al. 2023 [4]).
2. **Compute per-example gradients** g_t(x_i) = ∇θ L(y_i, f(x_i; θ_t)) (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]).
3. **Clip each per-example gradient** to L2 norm at most C: g ← g / max(1, ‖g‖₂/C) (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Annamalai and Cristofaro 2024 [5]). Clipping happens before averaging and bounds each example's influence (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Nasr et al. 2023 [4]).
4. **Add Gaussian noise** to the sum of clipped gradients, with noise N(0, σ²C²I). The result is divided by B (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Annamalai and Cristofaro 2024 [5]). Because the noise is proportional to C, each clipped example's impact is masked (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]).
5. **Update:** θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η·ḡ_t (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]).

The same clip-and-noise recipe yields private versions of other optimizers such as Adam and Adagrad (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Bu et al. 2022 [3]).

## 2. Practical points on clipping and noise
- **Cost.** Many autodiff libraries do not expose per-example gradients easily. Some implementations, such as TensorFlow Privacy, compute them one example at a time, which loses GPU/TPU parallelism. Computing them is generally the slowest part of DP-SGD (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [1]; Yu et al. 2021 [2]).
- **Noise scale.** The noise grows as the square root of the number of model parameters (Yu et al. 2021 [2]).
- **Parameterization.** Reporting σ and C separately makes the noise level more transferable across datasets. Privacy accounting must use the decoupled σ, without C (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [6]).
- **Choice of C.** A small bound distorts gradient direction, while a larger bound requires more noise. One heuristic is the median of the unclipped gradient norms (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [7]).
- **Alternative clipping.** Bu et al. propose automatic clipping, ĝ_i = g_i/(‖g_i‖₂ + 0.01), which removes the need to tune R (Bu et al. 2022 [8]). They report that this saves hyperparameter tuning cost by 5× for RoBERTa-base under ε=3 (Bu et al. 2022 [8]).

## 3. Privacy accounting
- **Per-step guarantee.** Each iteration is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism, which is subsampling followed by Gaussian noise. DP is immune to post-processing, so guarantees compose over iterations (Nasr et al. 2023 [4]). Mironov et al. show that the privacy cost per evaluation diminishes quadratically with the sampling rate. They give a numerically stable procedure for computing the RDP of the sampled Gaussian mechanism and prove a nearly tight closed-form bound (Mironov et al. 2019 [13]).
- **Naive composition is useless.** Summing the ε's gives ε ≫ 10⁴ for accurate neural networks. Tighter analyses prove ε < 10 for the same algorithm (Nasr et al. 2023 [4]).
- **Strong composition.** ε grows only with √T (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [12]).
- **Moments accountant (Abadi et al.).** It tracks the log moments of the privacy loss random variable, which compose linearly. It then converts the moments bound to an (ε, δ) tail bound via Markov's inequality (Abadi et al. 2016 [16]). Later work restated it in RDP, where D_α(f(D)‖f(D′)) ≤ ε defines order-α RDP. RDP is then converted back to (ε, δ)-DP (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [12]; Mironov et al. 2019 [14]).
- **Order of σ.** For (ε, δ)-DP, σ is typically of order Ω(q√(T log(1/δ))/ε) (Nasr et al. 2023 [4]).
- **Other accountants.**
  - Numerical PLD/FFT accountants compute the privacy loss more exactly (Lebeda et al. 2024 [9]; Gopi et al. 2021 [11]).
  - The GDP/CLT accountant is an approximation. Gopi et al. show that it can significantly underreport the true ε (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]).
  - Nasr et al. report that RDP and GDP give comparable bounds for MNIST (sampling rate 256/60000, 60 epochs) (Nasr et al. 2021 [15]).
  - Gopi et al. note that reducing ε from 2 to 1 can allow 4× more epochs at the same budget (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]).
- **Pitfall: sampling mismatch.** Most accountants assume Poisson subsampling, but many implementations use shuffle-and-partition batches. The hope that this mismatch has a negligible effect is an assumption, not an established result (Lebeda et al. 2024 [9]).

## 4. Worked example (tool computation)
These runs use Poisson sampling, add-or-remove-one neighboring, sample_rate 0.00427, 14000 steps, noise_multiplier 1.1, and δ = 1e-5:
- RDP accountant: ε ≈ 2.5926 (dp_accountant [T1]).
- PLD accountant: ε ≈ 2.3780 (dp_accountant [T2]).

For the same mechanism, PLD gives a smaller ε than RDP, which is consistent with the point that numerical accountants avoid the looseness of earlier approximate methods (Lebeda et al. 2024 [9]). These numbers come from the tool runs, not from the papers.

## Not covered
The sources do not give a full proof of the DP-SGD privacy theorem or the exact RDP-to-(ε, δ) conversion formulas. To go deeper, you could use the arXiv search tool to add papers on these topics.

answer:
## 1. The DP-SGD step

DP-SGD is a drop-in replacement for SGD that adds per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise (Yu et al. 2021 [1]). One iteration, following Algorithm 1 in Ponomareva et al. (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]):

1. **Sample a batch.** Each data point is included independently with probability B/N (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).
2. **Compute per-example gradients.** g_t(x_i) = ∇_θ L(y_i, f(x_i; θ_t)) (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).
3. **Clip.** g_t(x_i) ← g_t(x_i) / max(1, ‖g_t(x_i)‖₂ / C). This bounds each example's influence on the gradient, and it happens before averaging (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).
4. **Add noise.** ḡ_t = (1/B)(Σ_i g_t(x_i) + 𝒩(0, σ²C²I)). The noise is proportional to the clipping norm, so each clipped example's impact is masked (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]; Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [4]).
5. **Update.** θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η ḡ_t (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]). The same clip-and-noise modification can be applied to other optimizers such as Adam or Adagrad (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).

## 2. Practical notes on clipping and noise

- **Clipping trade-off.**
  - De et al. describe a bias-variance trade-off in C. A large C gives a nearly unbiased but noise-dominated update. A small C introduces bias, but the clipped signal is larger relative to the noise (De et al. 2022 [2]).
  - They cite earlier work that wide ranges of small C can work well if the learning rate is rescaled. They suggest this means reducing noise variance may matter more than reducing clipping bias (De et al. 2022 [2]).
  - A survey mentions a heuristic of taking the median of the unclipped gradient norms (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [4]).
- **Noise and utility.** Larger noise lowers leakage risk but can degrade accuracy, which is the privacy-utility trade-off (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [4]). Noise grows with the square root of the number of parameters (Yu et al. 2021 [1]).
- **Cost.** Per-example clipping is computationally and memory expensive (Yu et al. 2021 [1]; Ponomareva et al. 2023 [7]). Computing per-example gradients is generally the slowest part of DP-SGD (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).
- **Architecture.** Components such as batch normalization create dependencies between examples, which breaks the per-example sensitivity reasoning. Opacus disallows them (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [8]).
- **Microbatching.** If you clip per-microbatch average gradients, ε stays the same but more noise is added. The sensitivity becomes 2C, plus k times more noise per example (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [7]).

## 3. Privacy accounting

Accounting tracks the cumulative privacy loss over all training steps. It relies on composition and on privacy amplification by subsampling (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [10]). Analyzing DP-SGD means composing the privacy curve of one iteration with itself k times, where k is the number of training steps (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]).

**Moments accountant (MA).**
- Abadi et al. introduced it with DP-SGD (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [10]; Abadi et al. 2016 [14]).
- Composing directly from the (ε,δ) tail bound can be quite loose. MA instead computes the log moments of the privacy loss random variable, which compose linearly, and then converts the moments bound to a tail bound using Markov's inequality (Abadi et al. 2016 [14]).
- It applies to composing Gaussian mechanisms with random sampling (Abadi et al. 2016 [14]).

**Rényi DP (RDP).**
- MA was subsumed into the RDP framework (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]), and it can be viewed as an instance of RDP (Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [15]).
- Mironov notes that RDP analysis of Gaussian noise is particularly simple. A composition theorem can be proved from RDP properties alone (Mironov 2017 [13]).
- In practice, each mechanism is analyzed via its Rényi divergence at several orders α, and the RDPs add up under composition. The total is then converted to (ε,δ)-DP (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [9]).
- The conversion: an (α, d_α)-RDP mechanism is also (d_α + log(1/δ)/(α−1), δ)-DP for any 0<δ<1 (Stock et al. 2022 [16]; Jayaraman and Evans 2019 [15]).
- RDP gives strict upper bounds but may be loose (Li et al. 2021 [12]).

**Subsampling amplification.**
- Running an (ε,δ)-DP mechanism on a random subsample with rate q improves privacy to approximately (qε, qδ)-DP, as described in the survey (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [9]).
- In the hidden-state threat model, privacy amplification by iteration can improve bounds further. Cebere et al. state that existing theoretical results hold only for convex problems (Cebere et al. 2024 [6]).

**Other accountants.**
- *GDP/CLT.* It is asymptotically exact but only approximate for finite compositions (Li et al. 2021 [12]). Gopi et al. show it can significantly underreport the true ε (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]).
- *Numerical composition (PRV).* This approach gives both upper and lower bounds on ε (Gopi et al. 2021 [5]; Li et al. 2021 [12]). For p=1 there is an exact formula, δ(ε)=Φ(−ε/μ+μ/2) − e^ε Φ(−ε/μ−μ/2) with μ=√k/σ, used to validate the method (Gopi et al. 2021 [5]).

**Using the accountant.** Given the noise multiplier σ, sampling rate q, number of steps S and δ, one computes ε. For a target (ε,δ), the procedure is numerically inverted to find σ (Li et al. 2021 [12]).

## 1. The DP-SGD step

DP-SGD is a drop-in replacement for SGD that adds per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise [1]. One iteration, following Algorithm 1 in Ponomareva et al. [3]:

1. **Sample a batch.** Each data point is included independently with probability B/N [3].
2. **Compute per-example gradients.** g_t(x_i) = ∇_θ L(y_i, f(x_i; θ_t)) [3].
3. **Clip.** g_t(x_i) ← g_t(x_i) / max(1, ‖g_t(x_i)‖₂ / C). This bounds each example's influence on the gradient, and it happens before averaging [3].
4. **Add noise.** ḡ_t = (1/B)(Σ_i g_t(x_i) + 𝒩(0, σ²C²I)). The noise is proportional to the clipping norm, so each clipped example's impact is masked [3][4].
5. **Update.** θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η ḡ_t [3]. The same clip-and-noise modification can be applied to other optimizers such as Adam or Adagrad [3].

## 2. Practical notes on clipping and noise

- **Clipping trade-off.**
  - De et al. describe a bias-variance trade-off in C. A large C gives a nearly unbiased but noise-dominated update. A small C introduces bias, but the clipped signal is larger relative to the noise [2].
  - They cite earlier work that wide ranges of small C can work well if the learning rate is rescaled. They suggest this means reducing noise variance may matter more than reducing clipping bias [2].
  - A survey mentions a heuristic of taking the median of the unclipped gradient norms [4].
- **Noise and utility.** Larger noise lowers leakage risk but can degrade accuracy, which is the privacy-utility trade-off [4]. Noise grows with the square root of the number of parameters [1].
- **Cost.** Per-example clipping is computationally and memory expensive [1][7]. Computing per-example gradients is generally the slowest part of DP-SGD [3].
- **Architecture.** Components such as batch normalization create dependencies between examples, which breaks the per-example sensitivity reasoning. Opacus disallows them [8].
- **Microbatching.** If you clip per-microbatch average gradients, ε stays the same but more noise is added. The sensitivity becomes 2C, plus k times more noise per example [7].

## 3. Privacy accounting

Accounting tracks the cumulative privacy loss over all training steps. It relies on composition and on privacy amplification by subsampling [10]. Analyzing DP-SGD means composing the privacy curve of one iteration with itself k times, where k is the number of training steps [11].

**Moments accountant (MA).**
- Abadi et al. introduced it with DP-SGD [10][14].
- Composing directly from the (ε,δ) tail bound can be quite loose. MA instead computes the log moments of the privacy loss random variable, which compose linearly, and then converts the moments bound to a tail bound using Markov's inequality [14].
- It applies to composing Gaussian mechanisms with random sampling [14].

**Rényi DP (RDP).**
- MA was subsumed into the RDP framework [11], and it can be viewed as an instance of RDP [15].
- Mironov notes that RDP analysis of Gaussian noise is particularly simple. A composition theorem can be proved from RDP properties alone [13].
- In practice, each mechanism is analyzed via its Rényi divergence at several orders α, and the RDPs add up under composition. The total is then converted to (ε,δ)-DP [9].
- The conversion: an (α, d_α)-RDP mechanism is also (d_α + log(1/δ)/(α−1), δ)-DP for any 0<δ<1 [16][15].
- RDP gives strict upper bounds but may be loose [12].

**Subsampling amplification.**
- Running an (ε,δ)-DP mechanism on a random subsample with rate q improves privacy to approximately (qε, qδ)-DP, as described in the survey [9].
- In the hidden-state threat model, privacy amplification by iteration can improve bounds further. Cebere et al. state that existing theoretical results hold only for convex problems [6].

**Other accountants.**
- *GDP/CLT.* It is asymptotically exact but only approximate for finite compositions [12]. Gopi et al. show it can significantly underreport the true ε [11].
- *Numerical composition (PRV).* This approach gives both upper and lower bounds on ε [5][12]. For p=1 there is an exact formula, δ(ε)=Φ(−ε/μ+μ/2) − e^ε Φ(−ε/μ−μ/2) with μ=√k/σ, used to validate the method [5].

**Caveat.** Tuning hyperparameters on private data incurs extra leakage. Both De et al. and Li et al. state that their reported budgets do not include it [2][12].

question: Walk through DP-SGD: per-sample clipping, noise addition, and privacy accounting.
answer:
**DP-SGD overview**

DP-SGD is a drop-in replacement for SGD that adds per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise. These two steps limit and mask the contribution of a single example (Yu et al. 2021 [1]).

**1. Batch sampling**
- At each step, a batch (a "lot" in Abadi et al.) is sampled. For the analysis, each example is picked independently with probability q = L/N (Abadi et al. 2016 [5][8]).
- In practice, for efficiency, batches are built by randomly permuting the examples and partitioning them (Abadi et al. 2016 [5]). The privacy analysis assumes the sampling described above.

**2. Per-example gradient and clipping**
- Compute g_t(x_i) = ∇L(θ_t, x_i) for each example in the batch (Abadi et al. 2016 [8]).
- Clip each gradient in ℓ2 norm: g ← g / max(1, ‖g‖₂/C), with clipping threshold C (Abadi et al. 2016 [5][8]).
  - Gradients with norm ≤ C are preserved. Larger ones are scaled down to norm C (Abadi et al. 2016 [5]).
  - Abadi et al. motivate clipping by the need to bound each example's influence, since there is no a priori bound on gradient size (Abadi et al. 2016 [5]).
- Clipping happens before averaging, on each per-example gradient (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]).

**3. Noise addition**
- Sum the clipped gradients, add N(0, σ²C²I), and divide by the batch size (Abadi et al. 2016 [8]; Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]).
- Because the noise is proportional to C, it masks the impact of each clipped example (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]).
- Decoupling σ (the noise multiplier) from C makes the noise level somewhat transferable between datasets and models. For privacy accounting, use the decoupled σ without C (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [3]).
- Then take the step θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η·ḡ_t (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]; Abadi et al. 2016 [8]).

**4. Practical costs**
- Per-example clipping adds significant computational and memory overhead. The noise grows as the square root of the number of model parameters (Yu et al. 2021 [1]).
- Many autodiff libraries do not expose per-example gradients easily. Some implementations compute them one example at a time, which loses GPU/TPU parallelism (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]). Computing per-example gradients remains the slowest part of DP-SGD (Ponomareva et al. 2023 [2]).

**5. Privacy accounting**
- Because DP composes, an accountant tracks the privacy cost of each access to the training data and accumulates it over training (Abadi et al. 2016 [5][7]).
- **Moments accountant (Abadi et al.):**
  - It is a formal result. With sampling ratio q = L/N and T steps, the algorithm is (O(qε√T), δ)-DP for suitably chosen σ and C (Abadi et al. 2016 [7]).
  - It saves a √log(1/δ) factor in ε and a Tq factor in δ compared with strong composition (Abadi et al. 2016 [7]).
  - Their example is L = 0.01N, σ = 4, δ = 10⁻⁵, T = 10000. The moments accountant gives ε ≈ 1.26, versus ε ≈ 9.34 from strong composition (Abadi et al. 2016 [7]).
  - The survey notes that for a very small total budget, strong composition bounds can actually be lower (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [10]).
- **RDP accountant:**
  - Each mechanism is analysed through its Rényi divergence at various orders α. The Gaussian mechanism has a closed form (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [9]).
  - RDP composes linearly, by summing across steps at each order α (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [9]). The total is then converted to (ε, δ)-DP (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [9]).
  - One conversion is ε_DP = ε_RDP + log(1/δ)/(α−1) (Aguilera-Martínez and Berzal 2025 [15]).
  - Mironov et al. give a numerically stable procedure for the RDP of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism and prove a nearly tight closed-form bound (Mironov et al. 2019 [13]).
- **Other accountants:**
  - The GDP/CLT accountant is only an approximation. Gopi et al. report that it can significantly underreport the true ε (Gopi et al. 2021 [11]). Li et al. likewise note it underestimates (Li et al. 2021 [12]).
  - Numerical composition of privacy loss random variables (PRV/PLD) gives both upper and lower bounds on ε (Li et al. 2021 [12]). RDP gives strict upper bounds but may be loose (Li et al. 2021 [12]).
- **Calibrating σ:** given a target (ε, δ), Li et al. numerically invert the RDP computation to get σ from the sampling rate q and number of steps (Li et al. 2021 [12]).

**Computed example (tool results)**

I ran the accountants with sample rate 0.01, 10000 steps, δ = 1e-5, noise multiplier 1.0, Poisson sampling and add/remove-one neighbouring:
- RDP accountant: ε = 6.712756664482653 (dp_accountant [T1]).
- PLD accountant: ε = 6.187745006408129 (dp_accountant [T2]).

The PLD result is lower, which is consistent with RDP being an upper bound that may be loose (Li et al. 2021 [12]). These numbers use a different noise multiplier from the Abadi et al. example (σ = 4), so they are not comparable with it.

**Not covered:** the sources do not detail how to choose C, σ or the batch size in practice, or the utility trade-offs of those choices. The arXiv search tool could be used to find papers on those topics.

question: How do embedding inversion attacks (e.g., vec2text) work, and what do they mean for RAG systems?
answer:
## How embedding inversion works (Vec2Text)

- **Threat setting.** Hosted vector databases receive only embeddings of the text, never the text itself (Morris et al. 2023 [4]). The question is whether a third party can reproduce the original text from an embedding (Morris et al. 2023 [4]).
- **Formulation.** Morris et al. frame inversion as controlled generation: produce text that, when re-embedded, lies close to a fixed target embedding (Morris et al. 2023 [6]).
- **Iterative correction.** Vec2Text uses the difference between a hypothesis embedding and the ground-truth embedding to make discrete updates to the text hypothesis (Morris et al. 2023 [4]). Seputis et al. describe the loop as follows. An inversion encoder-decoder generates a corrected text x^(t) and tries to minimize the gap between the re-embedded hypothesis ê^(t+1) and the target e. Both are fed into the next iteration until a preset number of steps is reached (Seputis et al. 2025 [2]).
- **Access assumptions.** The attacker needs only black-box access to the embedding model, but must query it at every refinement step (Morris et al. 2023 [5]). A malicious user with access to the vector database and text-embedding pairs from the same model could learn the inversion function (Morris et al. 2023 [4]).
- **Search settings.** Morris et al. report that more correction rounds help monotonically with diminishing returns. 5 rounds recover 77% of the BLEU score, and 50 rounds do better (Morris et al. 2023 [19]). Sequence-level beam search raises exact-match scores by 2 to 6 times (Morris et al. 2023 [19]).

## Empirical results (reported, not formal guarantees)

- On 32-token inputs from a black-box encoder, Morris et al. report BLEU 97.3 and 92% exact recovery (Morris et al. 2023 [4]).
- On BEIR corpora not seen in training, the method still perfectly recovers some datapoints (Morris et al. 2023 [4]).
- On MIMIC-III clinical notes truncated to 32 tokens, Vec2Text recovers 94% of first names, 95% of last names and 89% of full names, with 26% of notes recovered exactly (Morris et al. 2023 [17]).
- Seputis et al. reproduce the main trends, with some diverging results that they attribute to differences in checkpoints and dataset splits (Seputis et al. 2025 [2]). They find Vec2Text sensitive to input length and less robust out of domain (Seputis et al. 2025 [13][18]).
- In their password extension, ada-ms-128 recovers 36% of "Easy", 22% of "Medium" and 4% of "Hard" passwords. gtr-nq-32 recovers none, for reasons the authors say are unclear (Seputis et al. 2025 [20]).
- Earlier work had recovered only an approximate bag of words (Morris et al. 2023 [4]). Song and Raghunathan's inversion reached precision and recall above 60% each at the word level (Song and Raghunathan 2020 [10]).

## What this means for RAG

- **Embeddings are not safe by default.** Morris et al. conclude that embeddings present the same privacy threats as the text they encode and should be treated with the same precautions as raw data (Morris et al. 2023 [4]). Song and Raghunathan similarly say embeddings should not be treated as "vectors of real numbers" when the inputs are sensitive (Song and Raghunathan 2020 [16]).
- **Outsourced vector stores are exposed.** The exposure arises when a service holds only embeddings, as in hosted vector databases (Morris et al. 2023 [4]).
- **Defenses studied so far.**
  - *Gaussian noise.* Morris et al. add noise λ·ε to the embeddings. With GTR-base and 10 correction steps, λ = 0.01 degrades retrieval (nDCG@10) by only 2% while BLEU falls to 13% of the original (Morris et al. 2023 [15]). Seputis et al. reproduce the trend, with λ = 0.01 best, but note that λ must be tuned carefully or retrieval suffers (Seputis et al. 2025 [18][13]).
  - *Quantization.* Seputis et al. test quantization as a hyperparameter-free alternative (Seputis et al. 2025 [13]). On ArguAna, for example, BLEU drops from 59.1 to 19.0 under Zeropoint quantization, while nDCG@10 stays at about 0.28 (Seputis et al. 2025 [20]).
- **Limits of these defenses.** Morris et al. only test noise against a reconstruction model trained on un-noised embeddings, and leave adaptive attacks and defenses to future work. They also note that training with noise could help Vec2Text (Morris et al. 2023 [5][15]). A low BLEU score does not rule out coarser inferences, such as clinical area (Morris et al. 2023 [15]).

## Not covered by the sources

- None of the sources evaluates Vec2Text end to end inside a RAG pipeline.
- Zeng et al. study a different RAG leak, extracting the private retrieval database through attacks on the RAG system. They also report that RAG can reduce leakage of an LLM's memorized training data (Zeng et al. 2024 [9][12]). The excerpts give no details on how this relates to embedding inversion.
- Quantitative results for adaptive attackers against noise or quantization defenses are also missing. I suggest using the arXiv search tool to add papers on these topics.

- A naïve model conditioned only on the embedding performs poorly. A multi-step method that iteratively corrects and re-embeds the text hypothesis works much better (Morris et al. 2023 [6]).
- At each step the model uses the difference between the hypothesis embedding $\hat{e}$ and the target $e$ to make discrete updates to the text. - Song and Raghunathan study inversion that recovers a set of words without their order. They use white-box optimization-based attacks and black-box learning-based attacks, and report precision and recall above 60% each (Song and Raghunathan 2020 [7][12]).

## How embedding inversion works

**Goal and early attacks.** Embedding inversion tries to reconstruct the text behind a dense embedding. Li et al. introduced GEIA, which treats inversion as generation. A generative decoder produces ordered text from the embedding, and the authors report that it recovers about 40% of named entities on PersonaChat and about 15% on QNLI, versus under 3% for the earlier baselines (Li et al. 2023 [6][26]).

**Vec2Text.** Morris et al. frame inversion as controlled generation. The system generates text whose re-embedding is close to the target embedding (Morris et al. 2023 [5]).
- The attacker has the target embedding and query access to the black-box encoder (Morris et al. 2023 [3]).
- An initial hypothesis comes from an unconditional model. A T5-base-initialised corrector then compares the hypothesis embedding with the target and makes discrete edits to the text. This is repeated over several rounds (Morris et al. 2023 [3][22]).
- With sequence-level beam search, a new generation is accepted only if its cosine similarity to the target embedding is higher than the previous step's (Morris et al. 2023 [22]).

**Empirical results (Morris et al.).**
- For 32-token inputs embedded with a black-box encoder, Vec2Text reaches a BLEU of 97.3 and recovers 92% of examples exactly (Morris et al. 2023 [3][5]).

- On MIMIC clinical notes, it recovers 89% of full names (Morris et al. 2023 [3]).

**Independent reproduction.** Seputis et al. replicate the key results in-domain and out-of-domain, with minor discrepancies attributed to missing checkpoints and dataset splits (Seputis et al. 2025 [8]). They also report that:
- Performance degrades when text length differs from the training length (Seputis et al. 2025 [13][23]).
- Password-like strings without clear semantics can be reconstructed (Seputis et al. 2025 [8][13]).
- More iterative steps and a larger beam width both improve performance, and prioritising steps is more effective at a fixed runtime (Seputis et al. 2025 [24]).

- **Iterative correction.** Vec2Text uses the difference between a hypothesis embedding and the ground-truth embedding to make discrete updates to the text hypothesis [3]. - **Cost.** The multi-step approach increases inference time [2]. It needs one query to the black-box embedder per refinement step [6].

- On 32-token inputs, Vec2Text recovers 92% exactly, with a BLEU score of 97.3 [1][3].
